Annexation is the act of one country, government, or authority formally taking over a territory and making it their own, permanently and officially. Think of it as one entity reaching out, grabbing a piece of land that was previously separate or belonged to someone else, and declaring: "This is now part of us."

The key word is formally. Annexation is not just physically controlling a place — it is officially and legally absorbing it into your own territory, changing its status on the map, and treating it as a permanent part of your own land.

Imagine you own a house, and the house next to yours is either unoccupied, disputed, or belongs to a weaker neighbor. One day, you put up a fence around their yard, declare it yours, give it your address, and start making rules for it as if it were always your property. You didn't buy it through a mutual agreement. You just took it and made it yours by declaration. That is essentially what annexation is — just at a political and governmental scale, involving territories, states, or countries.
What Makes Annexation Different From Similar Ideas

This is where many learners get confused, so let's be precise.

Annexation vs. Occupation. When a military force moves into and controls a foreign territory during a conflict, that is called occupation. It is temporary and does not change who the land legally belongs to. Annexation goes one step further — it is a formal declaration that the land now permanently belongs to the annexing power. Russia militarily occupied parts of Ukraine, and then formally annexed them — that second step is what makes it annexation, not just occupation.

Annexation vs. Conquest. Conquest is the act of winning control over a territory, usually through war. Annexation is what often follows conquest — the official paperwork, the declaration, the formal absorption. Conquest is the deed; annexation is the claim that follows.

Annexation vs. Merger or Unification. A merger or unification typically involves mutual agreement between two parties who both want to join together. Annexation, by contrast, is almost always one-sided — the stronger party decides, and the other side rarely has a meaningful choice. When two equals voluntarily combine, it is a union. When one forces the other in, it is annexation.
The Two Main Contexts Where This Word Is Used

1. International and Political Annexation

This is the most common and significant use of the word. It refers to one country formally absorbing the territory of another country or a disputed region. This is serious business in world affairs because it changes national borders, affects the people living there (their citizenship, rights, laws), and can trigger international conflict.

Famous examples include:

  • Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014, when Russia formally declared that the Crimean Peninsula — which was part of Ukraine — was now Russian territory. Most of the world did not recognize this as legal.
  • Germany's annexation of Austria in 1938, known historically as the Anschluss, when Nazi Germany absorbed Austria into the German Reich.
  • The United States' annexation of Texas in 1845, when the Republic of Texas — which had declared independence from Mexico — was formally incorporated as a U.S. state.
  • Israel's annexation of East Jerusalem in 1980 and the Golan Heights, both of which are disputed and not recognized by most of the international community.

2. Municipal or Administrative Annexation

This is a quieter, more everyday use of the word, but it follows the same logic. Cities and towns regularly annex nearby land — suburbs, rural areas, or neighboring communities — to expand their official boundaries. When a growing city in the United States absorbs a surrounding township into its city limits, that is annexation too. The city now governs that land, collects taxes from it, and provides it with city services. This type of annexation is usually done through legal and administrative processes, and is far less controversial than the international kind.
The Question of Legality and Recognition

One of the most important things to understand about annexation is that doing it and having the world accept it are two very different things. A country can declare annexation, but other countries and international bodies like the United Nations can — and often do — refuse to recognize it as valid or legal.

Under modern international law, particularly the United Nations Charter, it is considered illegal to annex another country's territory by force. This principle is called the inadmissibility of acquisition of territory by war. The reasoning is straightforward: if powerful nations were allowed to simply seize weaker nations' lands whenever they won a military conflict, the world would have no stability, no rule of law, and smaller nations would have no security.

This is why you will often hear phrases like "unrecognized annexation" or "illegal annexation" in news reports. The annexing country considers the land theirs; the rest of the world disagrees and continues to treat the original borders as legitimate. This creates a contested situation that can persist for decades or even longer.

That said, historically — before modern international law developed — annexation was extremely common and widely accepted as a normal consequence of war and empire-building. The Roman Empire, the Mongol Empire, the British Empire, and virtually every major power in history expanded through annexation. The moral and legal judgment placed on annexation is largely a product of the 20th century's effort to build a more rules-based international order.
The Effect on the People Living There

Annexation is not just about maps and borders — it profoundly affects real people. When a territory is annexed, the people living in it may suddenly find themselves under a completely different government, with different laws, a different official language being imposed, different citizenship rules, and different rights. They may be welcomed as citizens, treated as subjects, or persecuted — depending on the nature of the annexing power. This human dimension is why annexation, especially when done by force, is often considered a serious injustice.

Annexation is the formal, official act of taking over and permanently absorbing a territory into your own country, city, or governing authority. It is one-sided, it changes who governs a place and who it legally "belongs" to, and it can be either legally recognized (as in peaceful municipal expansion) or broadly condemned (as in forcible seizure of another country's land). It has shaped empires, caused wars, displaced populations, and continues to be one of the most consequential and controversial acts in world politics.
